q.intro.text: Maya bikes from Millbrook to Lake Camp on the roads: east on the highway, then north on the road. About how far does she ride? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The map moves first, then the board.

e.step0.text: The map key says a dot is a town, and a tent is a camp. Measure from the center of each symbol. The size of a symbol is not the size of the place.

e.step1.text: The scale bar is a number line: zero, two, four, six miles. Every interval is one inch long, and represents two miles, everywhere on this map.

e.step2.text: Lay copies of one interval along the road. Four fit along the highway: eight miles. And three along the road north: six miles. By road, fourteen miles.

e.step3.text: Straight across the lake, as the crow flies, only five intervals fit: ten miles. Maya can't ride across a lake, so her ride is fourteen miles.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is the trip by road longer than the straight line?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. A straight line is the shortest way between two places. The road bends around the lake, so it can only be longer.

e.why.wide.text: The width of a line only tells you the kind of road. Distance is measured along the line, and every inch is two miles.

e.why.scale.text: One map, one scale. Every inch represents two miles, on the roads and across the lake alike.

t.intro.text: Next day, Maya rides from Lake Camp to Pinecrest by road. Finding the places and reading the bar are done for you.

t.road.text: Copies of one interval are laid along the road. How many miles is the ride?

t.road.ok.text: Yes. Three and a half intervals of two miles. Three times two is six, and half of two is one. Seven miles.

t.road.whole.text: The last copy only fits halfway. Half an interval is one mile, not two.

t.road.drop.text: Don't drop the last half interval. It is one more mile.

t.road.count.text: Three and a half is the number of intervals. Each interval represents two miles.

t.road.miss.text: Count the intervals along the road, the half one too, then use two miles for each.

t.line.text: And as the crow flies, straight from the camp to Pinecrest?

t.line.ok.text: Yes. Two and a half intervals: five miles. The road is two miles longer.

t.line.road.text: Seven miles is the ride along the road. The straight line cuts the corner.

t.line.inch.text: Two and a half is the number of intervals, the inches on the map. Each one represents two miles.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked fourteen miles, and you were right. Now you can show why: lay the bar along the road.

q.cb.straight.text: At the start you picked ten miles. That is the straight line across the lake, but Maya rides the road.

q.cb.count.text: At the start you picked seven miles. That counts the intervals as miles, but each one represents two miles.

q.cb.none.text: Find the places with the key, read the bar, and lay it along the road you travel.

p.intro.text: Sam measures the trail from Millbrook to Pinecrest. He says: the bar ends at six, so each interval is six miles. The trail is five and a half intervals, and five and a half times six is thirty-three miles. Is Sam right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The bar counts zero, two, four, six. Each interval is two miles. Six is where the whole bar ends.

p.c2.text: Right. Copies of one interval fit along the trail: five and a half of them.

p.c3.text: Right. Five and a half times two is eleven. The trail is eleven miles, not thirty-three.

p.no.total.text: That is exactly Sam's slip. Six is where the whole bar ends. Each interval is two.

p.no.marks.text: Count spaces, not marks. Four marks make three intervals.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the map backs every one. Sam read the end of the bar as one interval.
